title: revocation-http: no URI filtering for SSRF
description:
pkix-revocation-http fetches whatever URIs appear in certificate CDP and AIA extensions (extract.rs). The crate's own rustdoc (lib.rs line 93-96) explicitly documents this as out-of-scope: 'No CDP / AIA URI filtering. This crate fetches whichever URI is in the certificate's CRLDistributionPoints or AuthorityInfoAccess extension. Restrictions on which hosts / schemes are acceptable for revocation fetches (e.g., enforcing HTTPS or blocking private-network URIs) are a deployment-policy decision and stay outside this crate.'

What goes wrong (integrity/availability): A certificate with http://169.254.169.254/... or http://10.0.0.1/... in its AIA/CDP extensions could probe internal networks via SSRF when the library is used in a server-side context. The library correctly filters to http/https schemes only (no file://, ldap://, etc.) but does not filter by destination IP or hostname.

This is documented and intentional -- the delegation to the RevocationFetcher trait is the right architecture. But callers may not realize they need to implement host filtering in their RevocationFetcher. A 'Security Considerations' section in the crate rustdoc would help.

Location: /home/mark/PROJECT/PKIX/pkix-revocation-http/src/lib.rs (documented at lines 93-96)
notes:
2026-11-24: independently reproduced while checking whether the IP-literal bypass found in pkix-aia-http (PKIX-j72x) also affected this crate. It does not -- there is no destination filter here to bypass -- and the same-origin redirect mitigation that makes the no-policy decision coherent is real and tested on both the ureq and reqwest paths, six tests, with the cross-origin cases asserting the internal server was never contacted. See PKIX-xbhc for that detail.

NEW ARGUMENT FOR THIS BEAD'S RECOMMENDED FIX. This bead predates pkix-aia-http's own destination policy and its async family, both of which now exist. So the workspace currently ships two crates with OPPOSITE defaults for the same threat, both fetching URLs from a certificate whose signature has not been checked yet:

- pkix-aia-http: default-deny non-public destinations, applied at DNS resolution time, with an opt-in escape hatch and a dedicated SSRF test suite
- pkix-revocation-http: no destination policy at all, caller vets

Neither is wrong on its own terms. But a consumer who learns AIA fetching is SSRF-safe by default may reasonably carry that assumption to revocation fetching, and nothing in either crate warns them. The Security Considerations section this bead asks for should therefore name the contrast with pkix-aia-http explicitly, not just describe this crate in isolation -- the inconsistency is the part a reader is most likely to get wrong.
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-11-24, by this bead's own recommended means: a Security Considerations section in the crate rustdoc. No code change; the architecture this bead called "the right architecture" is unchanged.

## What was written

A top-level "Security considerations" section placed BEFORE the API details rather than among the six other limitations, where it previously sat. That placement was the substance of the problem: the fact was documented, but in the one place a reader skims.

It says, in order:

1. Revocation URLs are not configuration. A CDP or AIA extension is a field of the certificate being validated, read before that certificate's signature has been checked, so whoever presents a certificate chooses the URLs this process fetches.
2. The concrete consequence, named rather than implied: a certificate carrying http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ will have it fetched by default, and on a cloud instance that endpoint may return credentials.
3. What the crate DOES guarantee -- HTTP and HTTPS schemes only, same-origin redirects only, bounded response bodies, a 30-second default timeout -- each verified in the source rather than carried over from the old wording.
4. The distinction that matters: those bound what an attacker can do THROUGH a fetch, not WHERE a fetch goes.
5. Where to enforce a policy (in the fetcher trait, or by vetting the URL, the latter being sound precisely because of the same-origin redirect guarantee).
6. Why filtering by hostname before connecting is weaker than filtering at DNS resolution: a name can resolve publicly when checked and to loopback when connected.

The README carries the same warning, since that is what crates.io shows.

## The cross-crate warning, which was the addition over this bead's original scope

pkix-aia-http fetches equally untrusted URLs for the same chain-building purpose and REFUSES non-public destinations by default. So the workspace ships opposite defaults for the same threat.

Both defaults are defensible on their own terms: pkix-aia-http owns its transport and so can own a policy, while this crate's transport is a caller-supplied trait and a policy baked in here would be one the caller could neither see nor override. The combination is the trap.

Crucially, pkix-aia-http's own docs contain a section headed "Design parallel: pkix-revocation-http" telling the reader the two crates intentionally mirror each other -- the same ureq dependency, the same response-cap pattern, the same construct-once idiom. That is exactly where a reader forms the belief that the defaults match. So the warning went THERE as well, immediately in that section, rather than only in this crate where someone who never reads it would not see it.

## Incidental fix

The README announced "Status: planned (not yet implemented)" for a crate at 0.2.0 with two reference HTTP clients, a sync and an async fetcher family, a pluggable cache and 135 tests. Corrected, along with the future-tense heading beneath it. A reader who believes the crate is unbuilt will not act on a security warning inside it, so this was not cosmetic. pkix-ac and pkix-composite carry the same claim and are genuine stubs, so theirs are accurate and were left alone.

## Verified

The three guarantees were each checked in the source before being documented, rather than repeated from the previous wording:

- scheme filtering in extract.rs, case-insensitive, HTTP and HTTPS only
- same-origin redirect policy in both clients/reqwest.rs and clients/ureq.rs, with reqwest's own default (ten redirects to any origin) actively overridden, and six tests whose cross-origin cases assert the redirect target was never contacted
- DEFAULT_TIMEOUT of 30 seconds and a response-size cap in both clients

fmt / clippy / rustdoc -D warnings / typos clean; 176 tests pass across the two crates.

## Not done, deliberately

No destination policy was added. This bead's own assessment -- that delegation to the RevocationFetcher trait is the right architecture -- still holds, and a policy baked into a crate whose transport is caller-supplied would be one the caller could neither inspect nor override. If the asymmetry with pkix-aia-http is later judged to be worth removing rather than documenting, that is a design decision deserving its own bead.
